reference_answer:
The assertion that an internal tensor product of two irreducible representations is always irreducible is false. First give the general tensor-square obstruction, without adding finite-dimensional or characteristic-not-two hypotheses to the question. Let F be the common field of the vector space, use the ordinary ALGEBRAIC tensor product V tensor_F V, and set T_g=phi(g) tensor phi(g). It is a representation because T_g T_h=T_{gh} and T_e=I.

Let S(v tensor w)=w tensor v, extended F-linearly. Pure tensors span the tensor product, so checking them proves S^2=I and S T_g=T_g S for every g. Define A=im(I-S). This is a linear subspace and is G-invariant, since T_g(I-S)x=(I-S)T_g x. Group inverses also give equality T_g A=A if that convention for invariance is used. This route never divides by2 or presumes distinct eigenvalues +1 and -1.

Choose a basis {e_i}_{i in I} of V, with two distinct elements e_1,e_2. The ordered tensors e_i tensor e_j form a basis of the algebraic tensor product. In a chosen ordering of I,
A has basis a_ij=e_i tensor e_j-e_j tensor e_i, i<j.
Indeed these span all images of basis tensors under I-S and are linearly independent because each selected ordered coordinate (i,j) appears in just one such vector with coefficient1. This works even in characteristic2, where the minus sign equals plus. In particular a_12!=0, so A is nonzero. Every element of A has zero diagonal coefficients, whereas e_1 tensor e_1 does not; hence e_1 tensor e_1 is NOT in A, proving A proper. Thus the tensor-square representation is reducible whenever dim_F V>=2, with no need to assume the original V is irreducible.

For finite d, dim(V tensor V)=d^2 and the basis count gives dim A=d(d-1)/2. This is an INTEGER count, not division by2 in the field. The fixed subspace B=ker(S-I) has a basis of the d diagonal tensors e_i tensor e_i and the d(d-1)/2 sums e_i tensor e_j+e_j tensor e_i for i<j; hence dim B=d(d+1)/2 over every field. For finite d>=2, both counts are positive and strictly less than d^2. These supply the question's requested finite-dimensional comparison.

If char(F)!=2, then A=ker(S+I), B=ker(S-I), the projections are (I-S)/2 and (I+S)/2, and V tensor V=B direct_sum A. This is the source's symmetric/antisymmetric proof in finite complex dimension. In characteristic2, however, +1=-1, so the two eigenspaces just written coincide with B, not with A in general. In that case A is a proper subspace of B (the diagonal tensors witness it), and the displayed half-projections/direct-sum proof is unavailable. For example, at d=2, dim A=1 and dim B=3, although the +1 and -1 eigenspaces are the SAME B. The invariant image A still proves the requested reducibility. No source notation for an antisymmetric eigenspace is silently redefined to avoid this distinction.

For infinite algebraic dimension kappa=|I|, the ordered basis has cardinality |I times I|=kappa, and the basis of A has cardinality |{(i,j):i<j}|=kappa, under ordinary infinite-cardinal arithmetic. The diagonal-plus-pair basis of B also has cardinality kappa. Thus dim(V tensor V)=dim A=dim B=kappa; a strict finite-style dimension inequality is impossible here. These are the actual requested dimension computations, not a claim of smaller infinite dimension. The explicit nonzero a_12 and excluded diagonal tensor prove strict subspace inclusion even though dimensions agree. Consequently the original proof-method phrase 'compute the dimensions to show' is satisfied by the correct finite comparison together with an explicit explanation of why equal infinite cardinal dimensions cannot replace the universal properness witness. It does not authorize a hidden finite-dimensional premise. This concerns algebraic tensor products, not completed Hilbert/Banach tensors or a closed-subspace-only irreducibility criterion.

To genuinely refute the student's claim about IRREDUCIBLE factors, one must also supply such a factor with dimension>=2, rather than choose a reducible V. Take G=S_3 and W={(x_1,x_2,x_3) in C^3:x_1+x_2+x_3=0}, with the coordinate-permutation action. This has complex dimension2 and is invariant. If a nonzero invariant subspace U of W contains x!=0, its coordinates cannot all be equal (over C, equal coordinates and sum zero would give x=0). Choose x_i!=x_j. The vector x-(ij)x=(x_i-x_j)(e_i-e_j) lies in U, so e_i-e_j lies in U. Permutations give all coordinate differences, which span W; hence U=W. Thus W really is irreducible. The two factors W,W are irreducible, while their diagonal S_3 tensor action has nonzero proper A of dimension1 and B of dimension3 inside dimension4. The same action of ONE g on both factors is the INTERNAL tensor product in the question, not an external representation of G times G.

The low-dimensional tail also needs correction. If dim V=1 with character chi:G->F^times, then V tensor V has character chi^2 and is one-dimensional, hence irreducible. It need not be the original representation. Over C, let a generator of C_3 act by omega=exp(2*pi*i/3); the square acts by omega^2!=omega. A nonzero intertwiner between one-dimensional characters is scalar, so it would force equality of those characters; they are inequivalent. In fact chi^2=chi iff chi is trivial, since all chi(g) are nonzero. Equality of vector-space dimensions alone does not imply representation equivalence. If V=0, its tensor square is0 and A=B=0; no nonzero proper subspace witness or ordinary nonzero-irrep assertion is made there. These boundaries preserve, rather than silently weaken, the original dim>=2 target. There is no circuit, finite-bit, source-paper/kernel or global alias conclusion.
